subtopic_detail: First line agent for epileptic spasms when hypopigmented macules point to an underlying neurocutaneous disorder
stem:
A 6 month old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents, who have filmed what they describe as him suddenly bending forward and throwing his arms out, over and over, in runs of twenty or so just after he wakes. He cries afterwards.

His mother says he used to reach for toys and babble but has stopped doing both over the past month. Under the Wood lamp you find four pale oval patches on his trunk and thigh. His neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable and his head circumference is on the 50th centile. An urgent electroencephalogram is reported as showing a chaotic high amplitude pattern with multifocal spikes.

data_table.Examination: Four hypopigmented oval macules on the trunk and thigh, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Development: Loss of previously acquired reaching and babbling over the past month
data_table.Electroencephalogram: Chaotic high amplitude background with multifocal spikes

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start vigabatrin as the initial agent and arrange specialist follow up
options.rationale: The hypopigmented macules indicate tuberous sclerosis complex, and vigabatrin is markedly more effective than hormonal therapy for spasms in that specific setting, with response rates well above those achieved in other causes. It is therefore chosen first rather than as a second line agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Start high dose oral prednisolone as the initial agent and review shortly
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy with prednisolone is the first line choice for spasms without an identified structural or genetic cause, and it would be right had the skin examination been normal. The neurocutaneous findings here shift the preferred agent. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Start sodium valproate and arrange outpatient neurology review in two weeks
options.rationale: Valproate is a later option with substantially lower rates of spasm cessation and carries hepatotoxicity risk in infants with undiagnosed metabolic disease. An outpatient timeframe also underestimates the urgency of stopping the spasms. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Start levetiracetam and repeat the electroencephalogram in four weeks
options.rationale: Conventional anticonvulsants including levetiracetam are relatively ineffective against epileptic spasms, and a four week delay allows continued developmental regression. The distinction from focal or generalised seizures matters because the drug classes that work are different. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

options.text: Observe without treatment because these episodes often settle spontaneously
options.rationale: Spasms do eventually remit but at the cost of permanent developmental loss, and the duration of untreated spasms is the strongest predictor of poor cognitive outcome. Observation is never appropriate once the diagnosis is made. (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile spasms)

explanation.summary: Epileptic spasms present between three and twelve months as clusters of brief symmetrical flexion or extension, typically on waking, and are far too often mistaken for colic or reflux until developmental regression brings the child back. The triad of spasms, the chaotic high amplitude electroencephalogram pattern called hypsarrhythmia and developmental arrest defines West syndrome, and time to treatment is the main modifiable determinant of cognitive outcome. First line therapy is hormonal, usually high dose oral prednisolone in Australian practice, except where tuberous sclerosis complex is identified, in which case vigabatrin is clearly superior. Every infant with spasms therefore needs a careful skin examination under ultraviolet light, since the hypopigmented macules of tuberous sclerosis may be the only external clue and they directly change the drug chosen.
key_points: Clusters on waking with developmental regression suggest epileptic spasms
Hypsarrhythmia on electroencephalogram completes the West syndrome triad
Hormonal therapy is first line except in tuberous sclerosis complex
Vigabatrin is the preferred first agent when tuberous sclerosis is present
Time from onset to effective treatment predicts developmental outcome
explanation.pearls: Vigabatrin causes an irreversible concentric visual field constriction in roughly a third of treated patients, so baseline and serial ophthalmological assessment is arranged and the duration of therapy is kept as short as the response allows.

sources.label: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome

subtopic_detail: Avoiding percutaneous sampling of a large intrarenal mass in a preschool child before definitive surgery
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3 year old girl whose mother felt a firm lump in her left tummy while bathing her two days ago. The girl has been well in herself, eating normally and playing as usual, with no fevers, bone pain or weight loss.

On examination there is a smooth firm mass in the left flank that does not cross the midline and moves little with respiration. Her blood pressure is above the 95th centile for age and height, and urinalysis shows blood without protein. Cross sectional imaging has been reported and the surgical team has been contacted. Her catecholamine metabolites are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Smooth firm left flank mass not crossing the midline, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows blood without protein, urinary catecholamine metabolites within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Large mass arising within the left kidney with a claw of surrounding renal parenchyma, no tumour thrombus in the renal vein or inferior vena cava, no pulmonary lesions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Percutaneous core biopsy of the mass to establish the histological diagnosis
options.rationale: Needle sampling breaches the tumour capsule and seeds the track, which upstages the disease and commits the child to flank radiotherapy she would otherwise avoid. Biopsy is reserved for unresectable or bilateral disease or when imaging suggests a different tumour type. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Percutaneous biopsy followed by chemotherapy before any surgical resection
options.rationale: This sequence combines the staging penalty of biopsy with delayed surgery and is not used for a resectable unilateral tumour. It carries the same track seeding problem as biopsy alone. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Refer for primary nephrectomy without a preoperative percutaneous biopsy
options.rationale: Imaging showing an intrarenal mass with a claw sign of surrounding renal parenchyma in a preschool child, with normal catecholamine metabolites excluding the main alternative, is sufficient to proceed to upfront radical nephrectomy, which provides both the diagnosis and the staging. Australian practice follows the North American approach of immediate surgery for resectable unilateral disease, with chemotherapy then guided by the operative stage and histology. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Start chemotherapy based on imaging alone and defer any surgical referral
options.rationale: Preoperative chemotherapy without histology is the European protocol approach and is a defensible strategy internationally, but it is not the pathway followed in Australian units for resectable unilateral disease, where upfront surgery preserves accurate staging. The two approaches differ mainly in whether stage is assigned before or after chemotherapy. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

options.text: Observe with repeat imaging in six weeks before deciding on any intervention
options.rationale: A solid renal mass of this size in a child of this age requires definitive management rather than surveillance, and delay allows local progression and metastatic spread. Interval imaging has no role once a solid intrarenal tumour is identified. (Source: eviQ: Wilms tumour)

explanation.summary: A painless abdominal mass in a well preschool child, often discovered by a parent during bathing, is a Wilms tumour until proven otherwise, and the key clinical discriminator is that it arises within the kidney and does not cross the midline. The main differential is neuroblastoma, which characteristically does cross the midline, encases rather than displaces vessels, produces a child who looks unwell and raises urinary catecholamine metabolites. Hypertension occurs in roughly a quarter of children with Wilms tumour through renin mediated mechanisms, and microscopic haematuria is common. The management principle that carries the most weight in an examination is that percutaneous biopsy is avoided, because tumour spill upstages the disease and adds radiotherapy to the treatment burden of a child who is otherwise highly curable.
key_points: Wilms tumour arises within the kidney and does not cross the midline
Neuroblastoma crosses the midline and raises urinary catecholamine metabolites
Hypertension and microscopic haematuria are common accompanying features
Percutaneous biopsy seeds the track and upstages otherwise curable disease
Australian units proceed to upfront nephrectomy for resectable unilateral tumours
explanation.pearls: Handle the abdomen as little as possible once a Wilms tumour is suspected and document that in the notes, because repeated deep palpation risks capsular rupture with the same staging consequence as a biopsy.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass in children

subtopic_detail: Timing of corticosteroid initiation in Duchenne muscular dystrophy while motor function has plateaued
stem:
You are the registrar in the neuromuscular clinic reviewing a 5 year old boy whose genetic testing last year confirmed a deletion in the dystrophin gene. His parents have read about steroids and ask whether he should be on them.

His mother says he still runs and manages the playground but he pushes on his thighs to stand up from the floor and asks to be carried on longer walks. Serial timed testing in the clinic shows his rise from the floor and ten metre walk times have been unchanged over the last three visits, having improved steadily before that. His cardiac and respiratory assessments are within normal limits and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Examination: Calf hypertrophy, positive Gowers manoeuvre, proximal weakness of the hip girdle
data_table.Functional testing: Time to rise from the floor and ten metre walk time unchanged across three consecutive visits
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram and spirometry within normal limits, dystrophin gene deletion confirmed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about corticosteroid therapy?

options.text: Defer corticosteroids until he loses the ability to walk independently
options.rationale: Waiting until walking is lost forfeits the main benefit, which is prolonging ambulation and delaying scoliosis. Steroids started after loss of ambulation still have a role for respiratory and cardiac function but no longer preserve walking. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Start corticosteroids only once his forced vital capacity begins to fall
options.rationale: Respiratory decline occurs years after the ambulatory phase, so using it as the trigger would delay treatment well past the window in which walking can be preserved. Spirometry guides later respiratory management rather than steroid initiation. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Avoid corticosteroids because the adverse effects outweigh any benefit
options.rationale: Weight gain, growth suppression, reduced bone density and behavioural change are real and require active monitoring, but the evidence for prolonged ambulation, delayed scoliosis and preserved cardiorespiratory function is strong enough that steroids are standard care. The adverse effects are managed rather than used as a reason to withhold. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Start corticosteroids at the time of genetic diagnosis regardless of function
options.rationale: Starting during the phase when a young boy is still gaining motor skills exposes him to years of additional toxicity without added benefit, since the gains continue regardless. The genetic diagnosis defines who will need treatment, not when it begins. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

options.text: Start daily corticosteroids now while his motor function has plateaued
options.rationale: The accepted trigger is the plateau phase, when motor skills have stopped improving but have not yet begun to decline, which his serial timed testing demonstrates across three visits. Starting at this point maximises the years of preserved ambulation and delays scoliosis and cardiorespiratory decline. (Source: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

explanation.summary: Duchenne muscular dystrophy typically declares itself between three and five years with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and a Gowers manoeuvre, and a markedly raised creatine kinase should trigger genetic testing rather than a muscle biopsy in the first instance. Corticosteroids remain the only intervention shown to prolong independent ambulation, and the decision that matters clinically is when to start rather than whether to start. Australian and international consensus times initiation to the plateau phase, identified on serial timed function testing as the point at which motor skills stop improving but have not yet declined, which usually falls between four and six years of age. Treatment brings a predictable burden of weight gain, growth suppression, reduced bone mineral density and behavioural change, so bone health, blood pressure, glucose and immunisation status are addressed before and during therapy.
key_points: Serial timed function tests identify the plateau phase that triggers treatment
Corticosteroids prolong ambulation and delay scoliosis and cardiac decline
Starting during the improving phase adds toxicity without added benefit
Bone density, growth, glucose and behaviour need scheduled monitoring
Live vaccines should be completed before immunosuppressive doses begin
explanation.pearls: Check varicella immunity and complete live vaccines before starting corticosteroids, because daily prednisolone at these doses makes subsequent live vaccination unsafe and varicella exposure then requires immunoglobulin.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Neurology Network: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection in established very preterm labour in a normotensive woman
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite reviewing a woman at 28 weeks and 3 days in her second pregnancy. She was admitted six hours ago with regular painful contractions and her membranes ruptured spontaneously thirty minutes ago.

Her cervix is now 5 cm dilated and the midwife expects birth within a few hours. She completed a course of betamethasone yesterday after her first assessment. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout the pregnancy, her reflexes are normal and her urine shows no protein. The neonatal team has been called to attend.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, foetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, cephalic presentation, clear liquor draining
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows no protein, full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her management?

options.text: Withhold magnesium because her blood pressure and reflexes are normal
options.rationale: Normal blood pressure excludes the seizure prophylaxis indication but is irrelevant to the neuroprotective one, which depends only on gestation and the imminence of birth. Conflating the two indications is the commonest reason this treatment is missed. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate only if she develops signs of pre-eclampsia
options.rationale: This restricts magnesium to eclampsia prophylaxis, which is a separate indication with a different rationale and dosing intent. The neuroprotective benefit is lost entirely if treatment waits for hypertensive features that may never appear. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Give nifedipine alone to delay birth and omit magnesium altogether
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not effective once the cervix is 5 cm with ruptured membranes, and its purpose is to buy time for steroids and transfer rather than to replace neuroprotection. Omitting magnesium forfeits a benefit that applies whether or not birth is delayed. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour and birth)

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate now for foetal neuroprotection before birth
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate given to women before 30 weeks when birth is planned or expected within 24 hours reduces cerebral palsy and gross motor dysfunction in the surviving child, and this benefit is independent of blood pressure. At 28 weeks and 3 days with a cervix of 5 cm she meets both the gestational and the timing criteria. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Defer magnesium until after birth and give it to the baby directly
options.rationale: The neuroprotective effect depends on magnesium crossing the placenta and being present in the foetal circulation during labour and birth, so postnatal administration to the neonate does not reproduce it. Neonatal magnesium is used for different indications entirely. (Source: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate has two entirely separate obstetric indications that share a drug and nothing else. As eclampsia prophylaxis it is given for severe pre-eclampsia to prevent seizures, while as a neuroprotective agent it is given to women in very preterm labour to reduce cerebral palsy in the child, with roughly one case of cerebral palsy avoided for every 60 or so women treated. The Australian guideline applies the neuroprotective indication before 30 weeks of gestation when birth is planned or anticipated within 24 hours, regardless of the cause of the preterm birth, the plurality of the pregnancy or the mode of birth. Administration requires monitoring of respiratory rate, reflexes and urine output, since toxicity manifests as loss of deep tendon reflexes before respiratory depression, and calcium gluconate should be available.
key_points: Neuroprotection and eclampsia prophylaxis are separate indications for the same drug
The neuroprotective indication applies before 30 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours
Blood pressure and proteinuria are irrelevant to the neuroprotective decision
Benefit requires antenatal administration so the foetus is exposed before birth
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output during the infusion
explanation.pearls: Loss of deep tendon reflexes is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity and precedes respiratory depression, so hourly reflex checks matter more than routine serum magnesium levels in a woman with normal renal function.

sources.label: Antenatal Magnesium Sulphate Prior to Preterm Birth: Australian Clinical Practice Guidelines
